biases.example: Willingness to donate roughly the same amount of money to save 2,000 birds as to save 200,000 birds from an oil spill.

biases.name: Selection Bias
biases.definition: Distortion resulting from non-random sampling, causing the sample group to be unrepresentative of the total population.
biases.example: Running an online survey to measure national internet literacy, which systematically excludes individuals without internet access.

biases.name: Selective Attention to Partner's Flaws
biases.definition: The post-honeymoon tendency to disproportionately notice, track, and dwell on a partner's negative behaviors while ignoring their positive actions.
biases.example: Noticing every single time your partner forgets to take out the trash while failing to acknowledge the meals they cooked for you all week.

biases.name: Selective Inattention
biases.definition: The conscious or unconscious blocking out of sensory inputs, ideas, or feelings that cause anxiety, discomfort, or distraction from a goal.
biases.example: Tuning out the ticking of a loud wall clock or ignoring distressing news broadcasts to stay focused on studying for an exam.

biases.name: Selective Perception
biases.definition: The tendency for personal expectations, beliefs, and interests to filter and shape how external stimuli are perceived.
biases.example: A fan watching a sports game and noticing every foul committed by the opposing team while missing fouls by their own team.

biases.name: Self-Relevance Effect
biases.definition: Memory is vastly superior for information that is directly linked or processed in relation to oneself compared to neutral information.
biases.example: Remembering a list of personality adjectives far better if asked "Does this word describe you?" during learning.

biases.name: Self-Serving Bias
biases.definition: The habit of attributing personal successes to internal traits or effort, while blaming personal failures on external, uncontrollable factors.
biases.example: Believing you landed a promotion entirely because of your brilliance, but blaming a failed exam on unfair test questions.

biases.name: Semantic Equivocation (Semantic Confusion)
biases.definition: Using a key word or phrase with multiple meanings ambiguously within an argument to mislead or obscure the truth.
biases.example: Arguing "Noisy children are a real headache, and aspirin makes headaches go away, so aspirin will make noisy children quiet down."

biases.name: Semmelweis Reflex
biases.definition: Rejecting new scientific evidence or knowledge because it contradicts established paradigms or accepted beliefs.
biases.example: Historic resistance by medical professionals to handwashing protocols despite overwhelming evidence of germ transmission.

biases.name: Serial Position Effect
biases.definition: The tendency to recall the first (primacy) and last (recency) items in a series better than the items in the middle.
biases.example: Studying a list of 20 vocabulary words and remembering only the top three and bottom three words during a quiz.

biases.name: Sexual Overperception / Underperception Bias
biases.definition: The tendency to systematically overestimate (overperception) or underestimate (underperception) another individual's sexual interest in oneself.
biases.example: Misinterpreting polite professional friendliness as romantic interest, or failing to recognize overt romantic flirting.

biases.name: Shared Information Bias
biases.definition: The tendency for groups to spend time discussing information everyone already knows rather than unshared knowledge held by single members.
biases.example: A hiring committee spending an hour discussing a candidate's public resume rather than unique feedback from an interviewer.

biases.name: Slippery Slope Fallacy
biases.definition: Asserting without sufficient evidence that taking one initial, minor step will inevitably trigger a chain reaction leading to extreme disaster.
biases.example: Claiming that allowing students to submit an assignment one day late will eventually lead to total academic collapse and no one ever graduating.

biases.name: Social Comparison Bias
biases.definition: Preferring job or award candidates who do not pose a threat to one's own relative strengths or standing within an organization.
biases.example: A manager choosing not to hire a highly skilled applicant who might outperform them or expose their weaknesses.

biases.name: Social Cryptomnesia
biases.definition: A societal tendency to forget the historical origins, key figures, and minority sacrifices that brought about major progressive social changes.
biases.example: Accepting modern workplace safety laws as obvious common sense while forgetting the labor activists who fought and sacrificed to establish them.

biases.name: Social Desirability Bias
biases.definition: The tendency of survey respondents to over-report virtuous traits and under-report undesirable behaviours to look good to others.
biases.example: Over-reporting daily exercise habits and under-reporting junk food intake on health questionnaires.

biases.name: Social Facilitation
biases.definition: The tendency for people to perform simple or well-rehearsed tasks better when in the presence of an audience.
biases.example: Running a faster mile time during a track competition with cheering spectators than during a solitary practice run.

biases.name: Social Loafing
biases.definition: The tendency for individuals to exert less effort when working collectively in a group than when working individually.
biases.example: Putting minimal effort into a group presentation project because you know four other teammates are sharing the workload.

biases.name: Source Confusion
biases.definition: Misattributing the origin of a memory, leading to distorted recollections where real events are mixed up with overheard stories, dreams, or media.
biases.example: Believing a scene from a movie you watched actually happened during your own childhood.

biases.name: Spacing Effect
biases.definition: Long-term memory retention is significantly enhanced when study sessions are distributed over extended periods rather than condensed into a short timeframe.
biases.example: Retaining foreign language vocabulary much better by studying 20 minutes daily for months rather than cramming for ten hours over one weekend.

biases.name: Spotlight Effect
biases.definition: Overestimating the degree to which other people notice and evaluate one's physical appearance, mistakes, or presence.
biases.example: Believing everyone in a crowded room is staring at a small stain on your shirt when almost no one notices it.

biases.name: Statistical Bias (Selection Bias)
biases.definition: Distorting data or conclusions because the sample gathered is not truly representative of the population being studied.
biases.example: Polling visitors leaving a gym to measure national exercise habits, resulting in an inflated statistic about average daily workouts.

biases.name: Status Quo Bias
biases.definition: Preference for maintaining the current state of affairs, even when making a change would be objectively beneficial.
biases.example: Keeping a bank account with high fees out of inertia, despite readily available cheaper offers.

biases.name: Stereotype Bias
biases.definition: Memory retrieval distortion where recollections are unconsciously altered to fit prevailing social, racial, or gender stereotypes.
biases.example: Incorrectly remembering a female doctor as a nurse when recalling a past hospital visit.

biases.name: Stereotype Threat
biases.definition: A decrease in performance caused by the anxiety or fear of confirming a negative stereotype about a group you belong to.
biases.example: Women scoring lower on a math exam when reminded of their gender right before the test compared to when no gender prompt is given.

biases.name: Stereotyping
biases.definition: Expecting an individual to possess specific traits or behaviours based solely on their membership in a particular group without individual verification.
biases.example: Expecting a computer science major to be introverted and obsessed with video games before meeting them.

biases.name: Straw Man Fallacy
biases.definition: Distorting, oversimplifying, or exaggerating an opponent's argument so it becomes easy to attack and disprove.
biases.example: Claiming that someone who supports reducing a city budget "wants to leave our neighborhoods completely lawless and unprotected."

biases.name: Subadditivity Effect
biases.definition: Judging the estimated probability of a whole event to be less than the combined sum of the probabilities of its individual, mutually exclusive components.
biases.example: Estimating the likelihood of dying from "any disease" as lower than the combined estimates of dying from heart disease, cancer, or stroke separately.

biases.name: Subjective Validation
biases.definition: Perceiving statements or coincidences as meaningful and true if one's personal beliefs demand them to be connected.
biases.example: Believing a random dream was a prophetic vision because a minor detail matched an event that happened the next day.

biases.name: Suffix Effect
biases.definition: A reduction in the recency effect occurring when an irrelevant auditory stimulus (a "suffix") is appended to the end of a spoken list.
biases.example: Decreased recall of the final word in a spoken list because the speaker concluded by saying "Done!" immediately afterward.

biases.name: Suggestibility
biases.definition: The incorporation of false information or leading suggestions from an interviewer into an individual's actual memory recall.
biases.example: A witness altering their memory of a suspect's clothing after a detective asks, "Did you notice the blue jacket he was wearing?"

biases.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy / Escalation of Commitment
biases.definition: The tendency to continue investing time, money, or effort into a failing project or relationship simply because of resources already committed.
biases.example: Remaining in a toxic relationship for ten years solely because you feel you have "already invested too much time to walk away."

biases.name: Surrogation
biases.definition: Conflating a metric chosen to measure a strategy with the strategic goal itself, treating the metric as the ultimate objective.
biases.example: A call center focusing entirely on shortening average call duration, resulting in employees hanging up on customers to hit targets.

biases.name: Survivorship Bias
biases.definition: Concentrating on successful individuals or items that survived a process while overlooking failures that are no longer visible.
biases.example: Studying successful college dropouts like Steve Jobs to conclude that college is unnecessary, ignoring dropouts who failed.

biases.name: System Justification
biases.definition: The psychological urge to defend, bolster, and rationalize existing social, economic, and political structures over alternatives.
biases.example: Opposing workplace reformations because "the current hierarchy has worked for generations," even when it harms individual interests.

biases.name: Systematic Bias (Regression-Based)
biases.definition: Systematic distortion in judgment occurring when targets of comparative evaluation are subject to uneven or asymmetric statistical regression effects.
biases.example: Evaluating employee growth metrics without accounting for the natural regression toward the mean of extreme performance scores.

biases.name: Tachypsychia
biases.definition: An altered state of perception where time appears to slow down or speed up significantly, often triggered by extreme stress, exertion, or trauma.
biases.example: A driver involved in a near-miss car accident describing the event as if it unfolded in slow motion.

biases.name: Teleological Bias
biases.definition: Over-attributing purpose, intention, or goal-directed design to entities and natural events that arose without conscious intent.
biases.example: Believing that clouds exist specifically to bring rain to crops and trees.

biases.name: Telescoping Effect
biases.definition: A temporal memory distortion where recent events are perceived as occurring further in the past (backward telescoping), and distant events are perceived as more recent (forward telescoping).
biases.example: Believing a major news event from five years ago happened just last year.

biases.name: Testing Effect
biases.definition: The enhancement of long-term memory retrieval achieved by actively testing oneself on material rather than repeatedly reviewing or re-reading it.
biases.example: Scoring higher on an exam by using flashcards to test active recall instead of re-reading class notes three times.

biases.name: Third-Person Effect
biases.definition: The tendency to perceive that mass media messages have a greater effect on others than on oneself.
biases.example: Supporting a ban on certain political advertisements because you believe they easily brainwash the public, while feeling completely immune to them yourself.

biases.name: Threat-Related Attention Bias
biases.definition: The heightened tendency to automatically detect, monitor, and prioritize threat-relevant stimuli over neutral or positive stimuli in the environment.
biases.example: An anxious individual instantly spotting a small spider in the far corner of a room while completely overlooking the surrounding decor.

biases.name: Time-Saving Bias
biases.definition: Underestimating time saved when increasing speed from a low baseline, and overestimating time saved when increasing speed from an already high baseline.
biases.example: Believing that accelerating from 70 mph to 80 mph saves more driving time than accelerating from 20 mph to 30 mph over the same distance.

biases.name: Tip-of-the-Tongue Phenomenon
biases.definition: The temporary inability to retrieve a specific word or name from memory, accompanied by the strong feeling that retrieval is imminent.
biases.example: Knowing precisely which actor played a role and describing their appearance, but being unable to articulate their name in the moment.

biases.name: Top-Down Attention Bias
biases.definition: The selective filtering of sensory information based on internal expectations, prior knowledge, goals, or conscious focus rather than raw environmental stimuli.
biases.example: Searching for a lost friend in a crowded stadium by scanning exclusively for a bright red hat because you know they are wearing one.

biases.name: Trait Ascription Bias
biases.definition: Viewing one's own personality, mood, and behaviour as flexible and context-dependent, while viewing others as rigid and predictable.
biases.example: Explaining your quiet behaviour at a party as "just feeling tired," while viewing a quiet peer as an inherently shy person.

biases.name: Travis Syndrome
biases.definition: The tendency to overestimate the importance, uniqueness, or superiority of the present era relative to historical periods.
biases.example: Declaring that current social media challenges represent a level of cultural decline never before witnessed in human history.

biases.name: Truth Bias
biases.definition: An implicit tendency to accept incoming communication from others as truthful, regardless of whether the speaker is lying.
biases.example: Believing a stranger's directions in an unfamiliar city without considering that they might be mistaken or deceptive.

biases.name: Turkey Illusion
biases.definition: Expecting continuous historical trends to persist indefinitely, failing to anticipate sudden, structural trend breaks.
biases.example: Assuming a booming housing market will rise forever because it has climbed continuously for five consecutive years.

biases.name: Ultimate Attribution Error
biases.definition: Extending the fundamental attribution error to whole groups-attributing an out-group's bad behavior to their nature and their good behavior to luck or chance.
biases.example: Believing a rival team won a match purely due to a lucky referee call, but losing to them because they are fundamentally dirty players.

biases.name: Unconscious Bias (Implicit Bias)
biases.definition: Automatic, underlying attitudes and stereotypes that influence understanding, actions, and decisions without conscious awareness.
biases.example: Making immediate, subtle assumptions about a job applicant's competence based on their accent or name.

biases.name: Unit Bias
biases.definition: The tendency to perceive a single unit or standard serving size as the appropriate amount to consume, regardless of individual appetite or needs.
biases.example: Eating an entire large portion of food served on a single plate simply because it is presented as a single meal unit.

biases.name: Value Selection Bias
biases.definition: Relying uncritically on pre-existing numerical data when reasoning in unfamiliar contexts instead of running new calculations.
biases.example: Using last year's outdated cost estimates for a new construction project rather than calculating current material costs.

biases.name: Veblen Effect (Snob Appeal)
biases.definition: A phenomenon in luxury economics where demand for a good increases as its price increases, because high cost signals high social status.
biases.example: Preferring a luxury designer handbag over an identical unbranded bag specifically because the $3,000 price tag communicates exclusivity.

biases.name: Visual Blind Spot (Scotoma)
biases.definition: The functional gap in visual perception caused by the lack of photoreceptors where the optic nerve exits the retina, which the brain automatically fills in.
biases.example: Closing one eye and moving a dot across a page until it temporarily disappears, illustrating that the brain normally seamlessly "paints over" this gap.

biases.name: Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)
biases.definition: The tendency to remember an item that stands out visually or conceptually from its surroundings better than non-distinctive items.
biases.example: Spotting a bright red word highlighted in a list of black text and remembering that specific word best.

biases.name: Weber-Fechner Law Effect
biases.definition: Difficulty in perceiving or distinguishing small differences between large quantities compared to the same absolute differences between small quantities.
biases.example: Easily noticing the difference between holding 1 lb and 2 lbs, but failing to notice the difference between holding 50 lbs and 51 lbs.

biases.name: Well-Travelled Road Effect
biases.definition: Underestimating the travel time for frequently travelled routes while overestimating travel time for unfamiliar routes.
biases.example: Feeling as though the daily commute home takes far less time than a trip of equal distance to a new neighbourhood.

biases.name: Women-Are-Wonderful Effect
biases.definition: A socio-cultural tendency to associate significantly more positive qualities and attributes with women than with men overall.
biases.example: Implicitly associating terms like "nurturing," "gentle," and "honest" more readily with female figures in social research.

biases.name: Worse-Than-Average Effect
biases.definition: The tendency to believe oneself to be worse than peers at performing tasks that are unusually difficult or unfamiliar.
biases.example: Assuming you are worse than average at juggling, ignoring that most people cannot juggle at all.

biases.name: Zeigarnik Effect
biases.definition: The tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than tasks that have been successfully completed.
biases.example: A waiter remembering precise details of an open food order, but completely forgetting the details as soon as the bill is paid.

biases.name: Zero-Risk Bias
biases.definition: Preferring to completely eliminate a small, specific risk rather than achieving a larger reduction in a greater overall risk.
biases.example: Spending a full budget to reduce a 1% hazard to 0% rather than reducing a 20% hazard down to 5%.

biases.name: Zero-Sum Bias
biases.definition: Incorrectly perceiving a situation as a strict zero-sum interaction, where any gain achieved by one party must come at a direct loss to another.
biases.example: Viewing a colleague's professional promotion as a personal setback, even when your own career trajectory is entirely unaffected.
